Erdős #251 38 pp Equations typeset from the exact TeX
PDFOpen the PDF · 38 pp TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis

A claim-bounded complete reasoning record for Erdős #251. It retains the prime-gap summation identities, rationality-to-shift reductions, small-mismatch consumers, coefficient countermodels, finite evidence, and all registered families. No theorem produces the required cofinal mismatch for the actual prime-gap series, so irrationality remains open.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #251, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #251, which remains open.

Introduction

Let 𝑝𝑛pn denote the 𝑛nth prime. Erdős Problem #251 asks whether

Π=∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑛2𝑛Π=∑n≥1pn2n

is irrational [1] . Bloom’s catalogue records the problem as open [16]. Numerically Π =2/2 +3/4 +5/8 +7/16 +11/32 +⋯ =3.674643966…Π=2/2+3/4+5/8+7/16+11/32+⋯=3.674643966….

Throughout the formal development the primes are indexed from zero, so that 𝑝(0)0 =2p0(0)=2, 𝑝(0)1 =3p1(0)=3, 𝑝(0)2 =5p2(0)=5, and the gaps are 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝(0)𝑖+1 −𝑝(0)𝑖gi=pi+1(0)−pi(0). In that indexing

Π=∑𝑖≥0𝑝(0)𝑖2𝑖+1,Π=∑i≥0pi(0)2i+1,

which is the convention every statement below uses; we drop the superscript from here on. The first values are

𝑖0123456789𝑝𝑖2357111317192329𝑔𝑖1224242462i0123456789pi2357111317192329gi1224242462

so 𝑔0 =1g0=1 and every later gap is even, the primes after 22 being odd. A second normalisation with denominator 2𝑖2i also occurs, and at every finite horizon it is exactly twice this one,

𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖=2𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖+1,∑i=0n−1pi2i=2∑i=0n−1pi2i+1,

the factor-of-two normalisation. A factor of two does not change rationality, so no result below depends on the choice; the identity is stated so that the indexing cannot drift silently.

Notation.

ℕ ={0,1,2,…}N={0,1,2,…} and ℕ>0 ={1,2,…}N>0={1,2,…}. We write 𝜑φ for Euler’s totient function, den⁡𝑞den⁡q for the denominator of a rational number 𝑞q written in lowest terms, dist⁡(𝑥,ℤ)dist⁡(x,Z) for the distance from a real number 𝑥x to the nearest integer, and Irr⁡(𝑥)Irr⁡(x) for the assertion that 𝑥x is irrational. A rational number is called integral when it is the image of an integer. A sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) is eventually periodic with period ℎ ≥1h≥1 when 𝑎𝑛+ℎ =𝑎𝑛an+h=an for every sufficiently large 𝑛n. A set 𝐴 ⊆ℕA⊆N has density zero when |𝐴 ∩[1,𝑥]| =𝑜(𝑥)|A∩[1,x]|=o(x), and a property holds for almost all indices when its exceptional set has density zero. A sum over an empty range of indices is zero.

Relation to prior work.

The passage from the primes to their gaps is already public. Tao recorded on the problem page that summation by parts makes the question equivalent to irrationality of ∑𝑛(𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛)2−𝑛∑n(pn+1−pn)2−n, and named the shape of the missing input as a sufficiently quantitative and uniform prime-tuples hypothesis giving statistical control of the binary expansion of about log⁡log⁡𝑛log⁡log⁡n consecutive gaps [17]. Theorem 3 below is that reduction in exact form, with the endpoint retained, with convergence supplied by an elementary bound, and with the statement checked by the Lean kernel. The elementary bound replaces the prime number theorem. No priority is claimed for the reduction.

Land has since posted a conditional proof of irrationality assuming Kuperberg’s uniform Hardy-Littlewood prime-tuples conjecture, together with a Lean formalisation of that conditional argument . His route constructs weighted prime-gap tails converging to 66 from above, imposes a consecutive quadratic prime pattern by a mixed prime-counting moment, and averages over later prime indices to control the unprescribed tail. Nothing in this note is conditional on a prime-tuples hypothesis, and nothing in this note proves the unconditional statement his argument would need.

Erdős stated on p. 93 of the 1958 article that ∑𝑛𝑝𝑘𝑛/𝑛!∑npnk/n! is irrational for every 𝑘 ≥1k≥1, and wrote there that the proof for 𝑘 >1k>1 is complicated enough that only the case 𝑘 =1k=1 is printed [1]. A proof of the full family appears in Schlage-Puchta’s Theorem 3, which gives the stronger statement that 1,𝑆0,𝑆1,𝑆2,…1,S0,S1,S2,… are linearly independent over ℚQ, where 𝑆𝑘 =∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑘𝑛/𝑛!Sk=∑n≥1pnk/n! . The catalogue entry still attributes the whole family to the 1958 article .

On page 103 of his 1988 problem paper Erdős separately stated the fixed-denominator problem: he could not prove that ∑𝑛𝑝𝑘𝑛/2𝑛∑npnk/2n is irrational for every 𝑘 ≥1k≥1, and wrote that the case 𝑘 =1k=1 was probably already very difficult. He also stated the variable-denominator expectation that ∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑛/(𝑔1⋯𝑔𝑛)∑n≥1pn/(g1⋯gn) is irrational whenever 𝑔𝑛 ≥2gn≥2 and 𝑔𝑛 =𝑜(𝑝𝑛)gn=o(pn) [4]. That expectation is false: Kovač posted a construction of such a sequence (𝑔𝑛)(gn) for which the sum is exactly 11, on 15 April 2026 . The catalogue record still repeats the refuted expectation without mentioning the counterexample, as checked on 6 September 2026 [16]; its warning that relevant literature may be missing applies directly to this omission.

Section 3 of the 1958 article proves a classification for the variable-denominator family, and the hypotheses matter. Let 1 <𝑞1 ≤𝑞2 ≤⋯1<q1≤q2≤⋯ be integers satisfying, for some 𝑘 >0k>0, the article’s printed condition (5), 𝑞𝑛 >𝑜(𝑛/log𝑘⁡𝑛)qn>o(n/logk⁡n). We retain that nonstandard asymptotic typography without imposing a modern quantified interpretation. Under its stated hypotheses, the article proves that ∑𝑛≥1𝑝𝑛/(𝑞1⋯𝑞𝑛)∑n≥1pn/(q1⋯qn) is rational if and only if 𝑞𝑛 =𝑞 𝑝𝑛 +1qn=qpn+1 for one fixed integer 𝑞 ≥1q≥1 and all large 𝑛n [1]. The denominators are nondecreasing, and strict increase is not assumed. The endpoint 𝑞 =1q=1 is attained: if 𝐺𝑛 =∏𝑛𝑗=1(𝑝𝑗 +1)Gn=∏j=1n(pj+1) then 𝑝𝑛/𝐺𝑛 =1/𝐺𝑛−1 −1/𝐺𝑛pn/Gn=1/Gn−1−1/Gn, so the corresponding series telescopes to 11. Neither this historical classification nor Kovač’s counterexample addresses the fixed-denominator dyadic series studied here.

There is also a genuinely adjacent proved dyadic theorem. If 𝑃(𝑚)P(m) denotes the largest prime factor of 𝑚m, Erdős and Pomerance proved that

∑𝑚≥2𝟏{𝑃(𝑚)>𝑃(𝑚+1)}2𝑚∑m≥21{P(m)>P(m+1)}2m

is irrational . Erdős and Graham record the complementary indicator on p. 62: equality of the two largest prime factors is impossible for consecutive integers, so its series is 1/21/2 minus the displayed one and is irrational as well. That is a theorem about a bounded prime-factor comparison digit sequence, and the numerators in ΠΠ are unbounded.

Two further results of Schlage-Puchta enter below. His Theorem 2 classifies rationality for numbers whose base-𝑏b digit string concatenates the representations of a slowly growing integer sequence, and is a different object from the tail criterion here; it was already pointed at this problem in the catalogue thread on 15 April 2026. His Lemma 4 is the input this note actually uses. It states that for every polynomial 𝐹 ∈ℤ[𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑘]F∈Z[x0,…,xk] which does not vanish identically, 𝐹(𝑔𝑛,…,𝑔𝑛+𝑘) ≠0F(gn,…,gn+k)≠0 for almost all 𝑛n, where 𝑔𝑛gn are the actual consecutive prime gaps [14]. Its proof runs through Selberg’s sieve. Sections 6 draws two consequences from it.

Problem #251 also appears as the unproved declaration erdos_251 in the Formal Conjectures repository [19]. Its zero-based Lean sum starts with the zeroth prime over 2020, so it is twice the displayed normalisation and has equivalent irrationality status; its proof is sorry.

The strategy.

The digits 𝑝𝑛pn grow, so the series is not a digit expansion in any bounded alphabet, and the standard rationality criteria for such expansions do not apply directly. The classical elementary criteria for series of this kind instead control irrationality through the growth of the denominators. Erdős and Straus named a sum ∑𝑘1/𝑎𝑘∑k1/ak over a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers an Ahmes series [5]; for such a series the condition 𝑎1/2𝑘𝑘 →∞ak1/2k→∞ is sufficient for irrationality, and it is sharp, since shifted Sylvester sequences grow like 𝐶2𝑘C2k for arbitrarily large 𝐶C and have rational reciprocal sum. Both statements and their attribution are recorded in the introduction of Kovač and Tao [8]. Splitting each term 𝑝𝑖/2𝑖+1pi/2i+1 into 𝑝𝑖pi copies of 2−(𝑖+1)2−(i+1) writes ΠΠ as a sum of unit fractions with repetitions, and the denominators occurring in it are exactly the powers of two. Even ignoring the repetitions the growth hypothesis fails by every available margin, since (2𝑛)1/2𝑛 →1(2n)1/2n→1, and every arithmetic constraint has to come from the numerators instead.

What replaces growth control is denominator control on the sequence of rescaled tails. Rationality of the sum is equivalent to an eventual integrality condition on differences of those tails, and that condition uses nothing about the numerators beyond the fact that they are integers. The condition does not by itself force the numerators to repeat: Proposition 26, applied to 𝐾𝑛 =𝑛Kn=n, produces the integer sequence 𝜅𝑛 =𝑛 −1κn=n−1, which is unbounded and hence not eventually periodic, and whose dyadic sum is zero.

Outline.

Section 2 proves the identity and the irrationality equivalence. Section 3 develops the tail recurrence and states the three exact criteria: pointwise shift escape, the free-pair form with a free offset, and the lcm diagonal. Section 4 gives the local obstruction, its signed normal form, the explicit remainder bound and one certified actual pair. Section 5 records the two denominator floors. Section 6 proves the four obstructions. Section 7 reports the two finite measurements. Section 8 states the remaining obligation. All declarations linked below are checked by the Lean 4 kernel against the pinned Mathlib revision at the formal-source commit ee650b32b8b2, and the pinned sources contain no proof placeholders and no project-defined axioms. The cited system paper identifies Lean 4 [10], while the Mathlib paper documents the library’s historical Lean 3-era architecture [11]; it is not authority for the current pinned revision.

Summation by parts, with the endpoint retained

Summation by parts trades a sequence for its consecutive differences. The form recorded here is exact: it carries no error term, it assumes nothing about the sequence, and it retains the endpoint term. No endpoint is absorbed into an estimate. For a sequence 𝑃P of rational numbers and 𝑛 ≥0n≥0 put

𝐷(𝑃,𝑛)=𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑃(𝑖)2𝑖+1,Δ(𝑃,𝑛)=𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑃(𝑖+1)−𝑃(𝑖)2𝑖+1,D(P,n)=∑i=0n−1P(i)2i+1,Δ(P,n)=∑i=0n−1P(i+1)−P(i)2i+1,

both empty, hence zero, at 𝑛 =0n=0. We call these the dyadic partial sum and the dyadic difference sum of 𝑃P.

Proposition 1 (finite summation by parts). For every rational sequence 𝑃P and every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝐷(𝑃,𝑛+1)=𝑃(0)+Δ(𝑃,𝑛)−𝑃(𝑛)2𝑛+1.D(P,n+1)=P(0)+Δ(P,n)−P(n)2n+1.

Proof. A routine induction on 𝑛n. At 𝑛 =0n=0 both sides equal 𝑃(0)/2P(0)/2. For the step, adding 𝑃(𝑛 +1)/2𝑛+2P(n+1)/2n+2 to the left and (𝑃(𝑛 +1) −𝑃(𝑛))/2𝑛+1(P(n+1)−P(n))/2n+1 to the difference sum changes the endpoint term from 𝑃(𝑛)/2𝑛+1P(n)/2n+1 to 𝑃(𝑛 +1)/2𝑛+2P(n+1)/2n+2, and the two adjustments agree. ◻

Formalised as the summation-by-parts identity. Nothing is assumed about 𝑃P: no positivity, no monotonicity, and no convergence.

Specialising to 𝑃(𝑖) =𝑝𝑖P(i)=pi, whose first value is 𝑝0 =2p0=2, and writing 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi for the zero-based gaps, gives the reformulation.

Theorem 2 (prime-gap reformulation). Let 𝑝0 =2,𝑝1 =3,…p0=2,p1=3,… be the primes in increasing order and 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi. For every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖+1=2+𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑔𝑖2𝑖+1−𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1.∑i=0npi2i+1=2+∑i=0n−1gi2i+1−pn2n+1.

Formalised as the prime-gap summation by parts, using the gap partial sum and the gap cast identity; the latter records that the natural-number difference 𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛pn+1−pn agrees with the difference taken in ℚQ, which needs 𝑝𝑛 ≤𝑝𝑛+1pn≤pn+1, the monotonicity step. The leading 22 is the first prime, not a normalising constant. At 𝑛 =2n=2, for instance, the left side is 2/2 +3/4 +5/8 =19/82/2+3/4+5/8=19/8 and the right side is 2 +(1/2 +2/4) −5/8 =19/82+(1/2+2/4)−5/8=19/8.

The infinite identity and the irrationality equivalence

Write

𝑢𝑛=𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1,𝑣𝑛=𝑔𝑛2𝑛+1un=pn2n+1,vn=gn2n+1

for the terms of the prime series and of the gap series, so that ∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛 =Π∑n≥0un=Π. The termwise identity 𝑣𝑛 =2𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛vn=2un+1−un is the dyadic discrete derivative. It expresses each gap term as an integer combination of two consecutive prime terms, so once (𝑢𝑛)(un) is summable the gap series can be summed by rearranging two copies of the prime series.

Theorem 3 (infinite prime-gap identity). Both series converge and

∑𝑛≥0𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1=2+∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛2𝑛+1.∑n≥0pn2n+1=2+∑n≥0gn2n+1.

Proof. The bound 𝑝𝑛 ≤1250(𝑛 +1)4pn≤1250(n+1)4 of Appendix 9 makes (𝑢𝑛)(un) summable, and 0 <𝑔𝑛 ≤𝑝𝑛+10<gn≤pn+1 then makes (𝑣𝑛)(vn) summable. The shifted sequence (𝑢𝑛+1)(un+1) is summable, so summing 𝑣𝑛 =2𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛vn=2un+1−un and using 𝑢0 =1u0=1 gives

∑𝑛≥0𝑣𝑛=2(∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛−𝑢0)−∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛=∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛−2.◻∑n≥0vn=2(∑n≥0un−u0)−∑n≥0un=∑n≥0un−2.◻

◻

The polynomial bound is checked here, summability of the prime series here, the summability transfer is the gap-series summability theorem, and the displayed identity is the unconditional prime-gap identity. The prime number theorem is not a dependency at any point.

Corollary 4 (exact irrationality reformulation). ΠΠ is irrational if and only if 𝑆 =∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛2−(𝑛+1)S=∑n≥0gn2−(n+1) is irrational. The corresponding zero-based series with denominator 2𝑛2n equals 4 +2𝑆4+2S and has the same irrationality status.

These are the normalised irrationality equivalence, the displayed-series identity, and the displayed-series irrationality equivalence. Concretely, Π =3.674643966…Π=3.674643966… is irrational if and only if 𝑆 =1.674643966…S=1.674643966… is, and neither is known.

The tail recurrence and the exact criteria

The series is not attacked directly. Suppose ∑𝑖≥0𝑎𝑖2−(𝑖+1)∑i≥0ai2−(i+1) converges with every 𝑎𝑖ai an integer, and rescale its tails by putting

𝑇𝑁=2𝑁+1∑𝑖>𝑁𝑎𝑖2𝑖+1=∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2𝑗.TN=2N+1∑i>Nai2i+1=∑j≥1aN+j2j.

Two facts follow immediately. First 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑎𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−aN+1, so moving one level along doubles the rescaled tail and subtracts a single coefficient. Second 𝑇0 =2∑𝑖≥0𝑎𝑖2−(𝑖+1) −𝑎0T0=2∑i≥0ai2−(i+1)−a0, so the sum is rational exactly when 𝑇0T0 is. This section studies that recurrence, assuming nothing about the coefficients beyond the fact that they are integers, and resumes the prime-gap instance at the end.

Definition 5. Let 𝑔 :ℕ →ℤg:N→Z and 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q or 𝑇 :ℕ →ℝT:N→R. Say 𝑇T satisfies the dyadic tail recurrence with digits 𝑔g when 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 for every 𝑁N. Write 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁σh(N)=TN+h−TN for the shift of length ℎh at 𝑁N, and call a rational number integral when it is the image of an integer.

These are the tail recurrence, the shift, and integrality. One small orbit is worth having in view. Take every digit 𝑔𝑁 =0gN=0 and 𝑇0 =1/12T0=1/12. Then the orbit is 112,16,13,23,43,…112,16,13,23,43,… and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =(2ℎ −1)2𝑁/12σh(N)=(2h−1)2N/12. The shift of length 22 is not integral at 𝑁 =0N=0 and is integral at 𝑁 =2N=2; the shift of length 11 is never integral. Nonintegrality at one prescribed shift length therefore does not imply irrationality.

Iterating the recurrence ℎh times multiplies 𝑇𝑁TN by 2ℎ2h and accumulates an explicit integer. Define 𝐵0,𝑁 =0B0,N=0 and 𝐵ℎ+1,𝑁 =2𝐵ℎ,𝑁 +𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1Bh+1,N=2Bh,N+gN+h+1, so that 𝐵ℎ,𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+12ℎ−1 +⋯ +𝑔𝑁+ℎBh,N=gN+12h−1+⋯+gN+h: the tail block.

Theorem 6 (block identity). For every 𝑁N and ℎh,

𝑇𝑁+ℎ=2ℎ𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁,hence𝜎ℎ(𝑁)=(2ℎ−1)𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁.TN+h=2hTN−Bh,N,henceσh(N)=(2h−1)TN−Bh,N.

Proof. A routine induction on ℎh; the step is one application of the recurrence together with the recursion defining 𝐵B. The second identity is the first minus 𝑇𝑁TN. ◻

Formalised as the iterated block identity and the scaled shift identity. The shift also obeys the recurrence in its own right,

𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)=2𝜎ℎ(𝑁)−(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1−𝑔𝑁+1),(1)(1)σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1),

the shift step identity. The free-pair criterion and the lcm diagonal

The escape condition quantifies over a fixed shift length. Freeing the offset gives an equivalent condition with a weaker-looking producer.

Theorem 8 (free-pair criterion). 𝑆S is irrational if and only if for every 𝑡 ≥1t≥1 and every 𝑁0N0 there are 𝑁,𝑀 ≥𝑁0N,M≥N0 with 𝑀 ≡𝑁(mod𝑡)M≡N(modt) and 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁 ∉ℤTM−TN∉Z.

By (3.1) the orbit reaches an index 𝑁0N0 beyond which the reduced denominator is a fixed odd 𝑑d; let 𝑡t be the multiplicative order of 22 modulo 𝑑d. For 𝑁,𝑀 ≥𝑁0N,M≥N0 with 𝑀 ≡𝑁M≡N modulo 𝑡t, the difference 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN is then an integer, contradicting the stated property at this 𝑡t and this cutoff. ◻

The offset 𝑀 −𝑁M−N is free, so one nonintegral congruent pair for each modulus and each cutoff suffices in place of a supply at a single fixed offset. The mechanism is exact: beyond a rational state with odd reduced denominator 𝑑d, the difference 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN is integral precisely when 𝑀 ≡𝑁M≡N modulo the order of 22 in ℤ/𝑑ℤZ/dZ, the free-pair lattice, so every rational orbit has a cutoff and a modulus at which integrality holds exactly on the congruence classes, the lattice corollary. The criterion for the actual series is checked as the free-pair equivalence, over the actual real tail recurrence. No antecedent for this packaging has been located; the nearest located neighbour is Schlage-Puchta’s Theorem 2 [14], which treats base-𝑏b digit strings formed by concatenating a slowly growing integer sequence under a rationality hypothesis, and is a different object, and the sweep of the dyadic tail-recurrence and Bézivin-style functional-equation literature has not been run.

The criterion rules out two shortcuts. For the actual prime-gap tail, Section 12.4 combines the prime number theorem with a first-moment bound to show that, under rationality, some tail value occurs ≫𝐶,𝑑𝑋/log⁡𝑋≫C,dX/log⁡X times in (𝑋,2𝑋](X,2X]; here 𝑑d is the eventual odd reduced denominator and 𝐶 >1C>1 is fixed. This is specific to the prime tail, rather than a consequence of rationality for arbitrary integer-digit orbits, and equal tails have integral difference, so they do not supply the free-pair producer. Also, under the free-pair lattice the difference is an integer whenever the modulus divides the offset, and an integer cannot lie in (12,1)(12,1), so the window component of the reduced event below is already a contradiction on its own. Both derivations are ordinary proofs, recorded in the extended record and not formalised.

A local certificate, and one actual pair

The classifiers reduce irrationality to a condition of infinite precision imposed on a complete tail. Inside ( −1,1)(−1,1) integrality is equality with zero, so on that range the shift step identity (1) turns simultaneous integrality of two adjacent shifts into a single comparison of digits. What this buys is a certificate attached to one pair of adjacent indices, whose verification already contradicts integrality there. The distance of a shift from the integers never has to be estimated.

What cannot supply the missing input

The counterexamples in this section test which information about the gaps could force irrationality. They preserve selected growth, residue and nonconcentration properties while changing the dyadic value. The sparsity result has a different role: it rules out a positive-proportion lower bound for the two-window event, while leaving sparse-witness arguments available.

Paired corrections and cumulative congruences

The sparse construction preserves cumulative residues as well as coefficient residues. Two adjacent corrections provide a free weighted digit while fixing their unweighted total. A third coordinate is needed to repair the cumulative residue before that pair. We account separately for its location, size and contribution to the series.

The pair identities, modular repair, and conditional interval filling are the elementary core in . The source does not itself establish the schedules (3)–(5), upper Banach density, or block-law transfer. Those parts are the ordinary proof above, not a new Lean or Comparator verification claim. Applied to prime gaps, the construction makes no assertion that the corrected cumulative positions remain prime.

Algebraic nonconcentration survives the rationalising perturbation

Fixed-block polynomial nonconcentration is a finer property than size and residue, but it too survives the bounded perturbation. The relevant input is Schlage-Puchta’s Lemma 4: for every polynomial 𝐹 ∈ℤ[𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑘]F∈Z[x0,…,xk] which does not vanish identically, 𝐹(𝑔𝑛,…,𝑔𝑛+𝑘) ≠0F(gn,…,gn+k)≠0 for almost all 𝑛n [14]. Say that an integer sequence 𝑎a has fixed-block nonconcentration when it satisfies that conclusion for every 𝑘 ≥0k≥0 and every nonzero 𝐹 ∈ℤ[𝑥0,…,𝑥𝑘]F∈Z[x0,…,xk]. The property transfers across bounded perturbations with no independence or randomness assumption.

Proposition 20 (finite counting for shifted gap differences). Write 𝑝𝑛pn for the primes indexed from 𝑝0 =2p0=2 and 𝑔𝑛 =𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛gn=pn+1−pn. For ℎ ≥2h≥2 and 𝑟 ∈ℤr∈Z, let 𝑀ℎ,𝑟(𝑁)Mh,r(N) count 𝑛 <𝑁n<N with 𝑔𝑛+ℎ −𝑔𝑛 =𝑟gn+h−gn=r. Let 𝑄𝑁,𝐻,𝑟QN,H,r count triples (𝑥,𝑑,𝑠)(x,d,s) with 𝑥 <𝑝𝑁x<pN, 0 <𝑑 <𝑠 ≤𝐻0<d<s≤H, 𝑑 +𝑟 >0d+r>0, and all four integers 𝑥,𝑥 +𝑑,𝑥 +𝑠,𝑥 +𝑠 +𝑑 +𝑟x,x+d,x+s,x+s+d+r prime. Then, for every 𝑁,𝐻 ≥0N,H≥0,

(𝐻+1)𝑀ℎ,𝑟(𝑁)≤(ℎ+1)𝑝𝑁+ℎ+1+(𝐻+1)𝑄𝑁,𝐻,𝑟.(H+1)Mh,r(N)≤(h+1)pN+h+1+(H+1)QN,H,r.

Proof. Windows of total span at most 𝐻H inject into these four-prime configurations; the sum of all length-(ℎ +1)(h+1) spans is at most (ℎ +1)𝑝𝑁+ℎ+1(h+1)pN+h+1, which bounds the number of larger spans. ◻

The finite shifted-count bound is unconditional. To deduce zero density one still needs, for every 𝜀 >0ε>0 and all large 𝑁N, a choice of 𝐻H making the right side less than 𝜀𝑁(𝐻 +1)εN(H+1). The adjacent case ℎ =1h=1 instead requires the corresponding three-prime estimate, because two of the four positions would coincide. The all-shift implication records these analytic premises explicitly; it supplies neither estimate and does not prove irrationality.

Theorem 21 (nonconcentration is perturbation-stable). Let 𝑎 :ℕ →ℤa:N→Z have fixed-block nonconcentration, let 𝐸 ⊂ℤE⊂Z be finite, and let 𝑏𝑛 =𝑎𝑛 +𝑒𝑛bn=an+en with 𝑒𝑛 ∈𝐸en∈E for every 𝑛n. Then 𝑏b has fixed-block nonconcentration.

If 𝐹(𝑏𝑛,…,𝑏𝑛+𝑘) =0F(bn,…,bn+k)=0 then 𝐹𝐞(𝑎𝑛,…,𝑎𝑛+𝑘) =0Fe(an,…,an+k)=0 for the tuple 𝐞 =(𝑒𝑛,…,𝑒𝑛+𝑘)e=(en,…,en+k), whence

{𝑛:𝐹(𝑏𝑛,…,𝑏𝑛+𝑘)=0}⊆⋃𝐞∈𝐸𝑘+1{𝑛:𝐹𝐞(𝑎𝑛,…,𝑎𝑛+𝑘)=0}.{n:F(bn,…,bn+k)=0}⊆⋃e∈Ek+1{n:Fe(an,…,an+k)=0}.

Each set on the right has density zero by hypothesis, and the union is over the finite index set 𝐸𝑘+1Ek+1, so a finite union of density-zero sets has density zero. ◻

Corollary 22 (nonconcentration does not force irrationality). Fix 𝑀 ≥1M≥1 and 𝐾 ≥0K≥0, and let 𝑏b be the perturbed sequence supplied by Theorem 18 at the actual prime gaps. Then ∑𝑛≥0𝑏𝑛2−(𝑛+1)∑n≥0bn2−(n+1) is rational, 𝑏𝑛 =𝑔𝑛bn=gn for 𝑛 <𝐾n<K, 𝑏𝑛 −𝑔𝑛 ∈{0,𝑀}bn−gn∈{0,M} and 𝑏𝑛 ≡𝑔𝑛(mod𝑀)bn≡gn(modM) for every 𝑛n, 𝑏b has fixed-block nonconcentration, and the cumulative sequence 𝑃𝑛 =2 +∑𝑖<𝑛𝑏𝑖Pn=2+∑i<nbi satisfies 𝑝𝑛 ≤𝑃𝑛 ≤𝑝𝑛 +𝑀𝑛pn≤Pn≤pn+Mn and hence 𝑃𝑛 ∼𝑛log⁡𝑛Pn∼nlog⁡n.

Proof. Everything except nonconcentration is Theorem 18 together with ∑𝑖<𝑛𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑛 −2∑i<ngi=pn−2. The perturbation takes values in the fixed two-element set 𝐸 ={0,𝑀}E={0,M}, so Theorem 21 applies to the actual gaps, which have fixed-block nonconcentration by Schlage-Puchta’s Lemma 4. ◻

Fixed-block polynomial nonconcentration, taken together with a prescribed finite prefix of actual gaps, a pointwise bound 𝑏𝑛 ≤𝑔𝑛 +𝑀bn≤gn+M, every residue modulo 𝑀M, positivity and cumulative growth at the prime-number-theorem scale, is therefore compatible with a rational dyadic value. Taking 𝑀M even also preserves eventual evenness. To preserve a prescribed modulus 𝑞q together with parity, take 𝑀 =2𝑞M=2q, with the corresponding pointwise bound 𝑏𝑛 ≤𝑔𝑛 +2𝑞bn≤gn+2q. The boundary is exact: the terms 𝑃𝑛Pn are not asserted to be prime, and the conclusion says nothing about constraints with a block length or a polynomial family growing with the index.

The two-window event has density zero

The same lemma bounds the event that the local certificate consumes.

Theorem 23 (sparsity of the two-window event). Fix ℎ ≥1h≥1. The set of 𝑁 ≥1N≥1 at which the three hypotheses of Theorem 10 hold for the actual prime gaps has density zero. For the same ℎh, the set of 𝑁N with 𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 =𝑔𝑁+1gN+h+1=gN+1 also has density zero.

Proof. For 𝑁 ≥1N≥1 every gap involved is even, so 𝛿𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1δN=gN+h+1−gN+1 is even. If |𝜎ℎ(𝑁)| <1|σh(N)|<1, |𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1)| <1|σh(N+1)|<1 and 𝛿𝑁 ≠0δN≠0, then 𝛿𝑁 =2𝜎ℎ(𝑁) −𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1)δN=2σh(N)−σh(N+1) lies in ( −3,3)(−3,3), so 𝛿𝑁 = ±2δN=±2. Apply Schlage-Puchta’s Lemma 4 at index 𝑛 =𝑁 +1n=N+1 with 𝑘 =ℎk=h to the two polynomials 𝐹±(𝑥0,…,𝑥ℎ) =𝑥ℎ −𝑥0 ∓2F±(x0,…,xh)=xh−x0∓2, neither of which vanishes identically: each of {𝑁 :𝛿𝑁 =2}{N:δN=2} and {𝑁 :𝛿𝑁 = −2}{N:δN=−2} has density zero, and the event is contained in their union. The second assertion is the same lemma applied to 𝐹(𝑥0,…,𝑥ℎ) =𝑥ℎ −𝑥0F(x0,…,xh)=xh−x0. ◻

The two halves point in opposite directions and both are useful. The mismatch hypothesis on its own holds for almost all 𝑁N, which is strictly stronger than the cofinal statement Proposition 12 supplies. The full conjunction is confined to a set of density zero, because the two window conditions force the mismatch to be exactly ±2±2. A producer for Problem 29 therefore has to be a cofinality statement about a sparse set. Consequently, this event cannot be supplied on a set of positive lower density. A sufficient producer would have to yield cofinally many witnesses in a density-zero set; density zero alone does not exclude an averaging argument capable of detecting such sparse witnesses. The measurement reported in Section 7 is consistent with this: the observed density at ℎ =1h=1 declines like 1/log⁡𝑝1/log⁡p, and the observed count up to 𝑋X grows like 𝑋/(log⁡𝑋)2X/(log⁡X)2.

Recurring gap values differing by two do not suffice

Theorem 13 reduces the producer to a ±2±2 mismatch together with a half-window condition. It is tempting to hope that the mismatch half is the substance, and that two even values differing by 22, each occurring infinitely often as a consecutive prime gap inside a common index residue class, would suffice. At the level of integer-digit recurrences that implication is false, and it stays false under growth at the scale the primes actually have.

Theorem 24 (recurring values are not enough). There is a sequence (𝑎𝑛)𝑛≥1(an)n≥1 of positive even integers with the following properties. The values 22 and 44 each occur infinitely often at indices divisible by every fixed 𝑡 ≥1t≥1. The sequence is unbounded, not eventually periodic, and satisfies 𝑎𝑛 =𝑂(log⁡𝑛)an=O(log⁡n). The series ∑𝑛≥1𝑎𝑛2−𝑛∑n≥1an2−n equals 66, and every scaled tail ∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2−𝑗∑j≥1aN+j2−j is an integer, so every tail shift is integral. The increasing odd sequence 𝑃𝑛 =3 +∑𝑗≤𝑛𝑎𝑗Pn=3+∑j≤naj satisfies 𝑃𝑛 ∼𝑛log⁡𝑛Pn∼nlog⁡n.

Call an index 𝑛n special when 𝑛 =𝑘!n=k! or 𝑛 =2 𝑘!n=2k! for some 𝑘 ≥5k≥5, and define

𝑈𝑛={2𝑏𝑛−1−2,𝑛=𝑘!, 𝑘≥5,2𝑏𝑛−1−4,𝑛=2𝑘!, 𝑘≥5,𝑏𝑛,otherwise,𝑎𝑛=2𝑈𝑛−1−𝑈𝑛(𝑛≥1).Un={2bn−1−2,n=k!, k≥5,2bn−1−4,n=2k!, k≥5,bn,otherwise,an=2Un−1−Un(n≥1).

The factorial schedule above proves recurrence in the zero residue class. The following separate construction strengthens this to every residue class.

A complete countermodel in every residue class

There is a synthetic integer sequence (𝑎𝑛)𝑛≥1(an)n≥1 with all of the following properties. Each 𝑎𝑛an is positive and divisible by 22, and

𝑎𝑛≤4log⁡(𝑛+1)+24.an≤4log⁡(n+1)+24.

For every integer 𝐵B and cutoff 𝑁N, some 𝑛 ≥𝑁n≥N satisfies 𝑎𝑛 >𝐵an>B. For every ℎ ≥1h≥1 there is no cutoff after which 𝑎𝑛+ℎ =𝑎𝑛an+h=an for all 𝑛n. Nevertheless, all the complete tails

𝑈𝑁=∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2𝑗(𝑁≥0)UN=∑j≥1aN+j2j(N≥0)

are integers, 𝑈0 =6U0=6, and 𝑈𝑁+ℎ −𝑈𝑁 ∈ℤUN+h−UN∈Z for every 𝑁,ℎ ≥0N,h≥0. The sequence

𝑃𝑁=3+𝑁∑𝑗=1𝑎𝑗PN=3+∑j=1Naj

is strictly increasing and odd, with 𝑃𝑁/(𝑁log⁡𝑁) →1PN/(Nlog⁡N)→1. These are synthetic positions; no 𝑃𝑁PN is asserted to be prime.

To obtain every residue class, enumerate triples consisting of a positive modulus, a residue, and a repetition index. Choose the corresponding centres 𝑐𝑘ck in the prescribed classes with 𝑐0 ≥100c0≥100, 𝑐𝑘+1 ≥𝑐𝑘 +3ck+1≥ck+3 and 𝑐𝑘 ≥2𝑘2ck≥2k2 for 𝑘 ≥1k≥1. The parity of the repetition index selects the desired value 𝑣𝑘 =2vk=2 or 44. Use the even baseline

𝑏𝑛=6+2⌊log⁡(𝑛+1)2⌋,𝑈𝑛={2𝑏𝑛−1−𝑣𝑘,𝑛=𝑐𝑘,𝑏𝑛,𝑛∉{𝑐𝑘:𝑘≥0},bn=6+2⌊log⁡(n+1)2⌋,Un={2bn−1−vk,n=ck,bn,n∉{ck:k≥0},

and define 𝑎𝑛 =2𝑈𝑛−1 −𝑈𝑛an=2Un−1−Un. The separation of the centres and the baseline increment bound give positivity and the displayed logarithmic bound. Finite telescoping leaves 𝑈𝑁+𝑚/2𝑚UN+m/2m, which tends to zero; thus these carries are the complete tails. The sparse changes to the baseline have negligible contribution after division by 𝑁log⁡𝑁Nlog⁡N, which gives the stated growth of 𝑃𝑁PN.

The full statement is kernel-checked in Lean.

This rules out an inference from these coefficient properties alone to nonintegral tail shifts. It gives no counterexample to the prime-gap problem and does not reproduce the extreme large gaps of the primes.

The consequence is exact. Positivity, evenness, unboundedness, non-eventual periodicity, a pointwise logarithmic bound, cumulative growth at the prime-number-theorem scale, and the recurrence of two even values differing by 22 inside every index residue class are jointly compatible with an integral tail at every index. Any route through that input must use a property of the consecutive primes beyond this list. The sequence (𝑎𝑛)(an) is synthetic and the 𝑃𝑛Pn are not asserted to be prime. The pointwise logarithmic bound also precludes the known large-gap behaviour, so the theorem does not speak to hypotheses that use extreme gaps.

Two further boundaries

Proposition 25 (quadratic polynomial-shift countermodel). Put 𝑐𝑛 =2(𝑛2 +4𝑛 +2)cn=2(n2+4n+2) and 𝑈𝑛 =2(𝑛 +4)2Un=2(n+4)2. Then 𝑐𝑛cn is positive, even and strictly increasing, 𝑈𝑛+1 =2𝑈𝑛 −𝑐𝑛+1Un+1=2Un−cn+1, every shift 𝑈𝑁+ℎ −𝑈𝑁UN+h−UN is integral, 𝑐𝑛+1 −𝑐𝑛 =4𝑛 +10cn+1−cn=4n+10 is never ±2±2, and

∑𝑗≥1𝑐𝑗2𝑗=32.∑j≥1cj2j=32.

Proof. Direct expansion gives the recurrence, and the finite telescope is ∑𝑛𝑗=1𝑐𝑗2−𝑗 =32 −2(𝑛 +4)22−𝑛∑j=1ncj2−j=32−2(n+4)22−n, whose last term tends to zero. The remaining assertions follow from the integer values of 𝑈𝑛Un and from 𝑐𝑛+1 −𝑐𝑛 =4𝑛 +10 ≥10cn+1−cn=4n+10≥10. ◻

The series is the one starting at 𝑗 =1j=1, whose initial tail state is 𝑈0 =32U0=32; under the opening convention ∑𝑛≥0𝑐𝑛2−(𝑛+1)∑n≥0cn2−(n+1) the same word has value 1818, and the two ranges must be kept apart. The formal construction checks the recurrence, strict growth, integrality of every shift, exclusion of adjacent differences of size two, and the value 3232 for the shifted series, whose summand is 𝑐𝑛+1/2𝑛+1cn+1/2n+1; the rational value is recorded at line 109. Positivity, parity, strict growth, unboundedness and nonperiodicity are therefore jointly compatible with rationality, and the adjacent trigger of Theorem 13 fails at every index. The telescoping mechanism is the one Kovač used against the variable-denominator conjecture printed under the problem ; the word carries no priority claim and is not a result about Problem #251.

Rationality also fails to force the coefficients to repeat. Let 𝐾 :ℕ →ℚK:N→Q be arbitrary and put 𝜅𝑛 =2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1κn=2Kn−Kn+1: the carry coefficient.

Proposition 26 (exact telescoping). For every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0, ∑𝑛−1𝑖=0𝜅𝑖2−(𝑖+1) =𝐾0 −𝐾𝑛2−𝑛∑i=0n−1κi2−(i+1)=K0−Kn2−n.

Proof. A routine induction; the added term is (2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1)2−(𝑛+1) =𝐾𝑛2−𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+12−(𝑛+1)(2Kn−Kn+1)2−(n+1)=Kn2−n−Kn+12−(n+1). ◻

Formalised as the carry telescoping identity. Taking 𝐾0 =52K0=52 and 𝐾𝑛 =2𝑛 +2Kn=2n+2 for 𝑛 ≥1n≥1 gives 𝜅0 =1κ0=1 and 𝜅𝑛 =2𝑛κn=2n, so the coefficients 1,2,4,6,8,…1,2,4,6,8,… are positive, even after the first term, unbounded and not eventually periodic, while their dyadic sum is 5252. Rationality alone therefore cannot imply eventual periodicity even for a positive, parity-correct integer coefficient sequence, and no argument may play periodicity of a rational value against Proposition 12.

Finally, two escape tests that look like independent producers are equivalent to the conclusion they were introduced to supply. For fixed ℎh write 𝛿𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1δN=gN+h+1−gN+1, 𝐷𝑁 =𝜎ℎ(𝑁)DN=σh(N) and 𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 =∑𝑟−1𝑖=02𝑟−1−𝑖𝛿𝑁+𝑖Bh,N,r=∑i=0r−12r−1−iδN+i, so that 𝐷𝑁+𝑟 =2𝑟𝐷𝑁 −𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟DN+r=2rDN−Bh,N,r, and call the data-dependent affine condition A𝑁,𝑟AN,r the assertion 𝐷𝑁+𝑟 ∈ −𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 +2𝑟+1ℤDN+r∈−Bh,N,r+2r+1Z.

Theorem 27 (affine and fixed-lattice circularity). For every rational dyadic tail recurrence and all ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 ≥0h,N,r≥0, A𝑁,𝑟AN,r holds if and only if 𝐷𝑁 ∈2ℤDN∈2Z. Consequently, if every 𝛿𝑁δN is even, cofinal failure of AA is equivalent to nonintegrality of 𝐷𝑁DN for arbitrarily large 𝑁N. The same equivalence holds for the fixed-lattice replacement, under any bound |𝐷𝑁| ≤𝑏(𝑁)|DN|≤b(N) satisfying 2𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)𝑞 <2𝑟2b(N+r)q<2r for some 𝑟r at every 𝑁N and every positive integer 𝑞q.

Proof. Substituting 𝐷𝑁+𝑟 =2𝑟𝐷𝑁 −𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟DN+r=2rDN−Bh,N,r into A𝑁,𝑟AN,r cancels the observed block and leaves 𝐷𝑁 =2𝑧DN=2z. After one recurrence step, evenness of 𝛿𝑁δN identifies even integrality at 𝑁 +1N+1 with ordinary integrality at 𝑁N; the reverse implication chooses a nonintegral 𝐷𝑁DN and depth 𝑟 =0r=0. For the fixed-lattice form, eventual integrality and the block identity give 𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 −2𝑟𝑧 = −𝐷𝑁+𝑟Bh,N,r−2rz=−DN+r, so a strict separation exceeding 𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)b(N+r) is contradictory; conversely a nonintegral 𝐷𝑁DN with reduced denominator 𝑞q has distance at least 1/𝑞1/q from every integer, and scaling that separation by 2𝑟2r at a legal depth gives the required strict inequality. ◻

These are the pointwise affine identity, its cofinal form, and the fixed-lattice equivalence. The apparent affine hierarchy contains no depth-dependent information, and the fixed lattice removes the data dependence at the cost of a growth condition under which rational denominator separation already forces every required escape. Neither is an independent source of information about consecutive primes.

What is measured

Two finite computations report on the two producers. Each covers one bounded range and supplies no cofinal statement.

Over the 6 841 6486841648 primes below 1.2 ×1081.2×108 and offsets ℎ =1,…,16h=1,…,16, the reduced two-window event of Theorem 13 occurs at every offset, with density between 0.004180.00418 and 0.0082480.008248 and the two signs near balanced; at ℎ =1h=1 there are 56 42756427 occurrences among 6 841 5646841564 candidate indices, the last at the prime 119 995 753119995753. Rescaled by log⁡𝑝log⁡p the band densities run from 0.176710.17671 down to 0.131480.13148 with decelerating drift over the measured bands. This finite observation does not establish an asymptotic counting law or cofinality. The tails in this scan are double-precision floating-point, so an individual hit is a numerical observation and carries no certificate; the median distance from the shift to the nearer window boundary is 0.1270.127 and the worst case over 34 00034000 hits is 6.1 ×10−76.1×10−7, eight orders above the working resolution, and 3 2003200 sampled hits across ℎ =1,…,8h=1,…,8 were rechecked against the literal three-part statement with no violations. Proposition 15 is the one pair certified by exact integer arithmetic. The receipt is adjacent-mismatch.json.

Over the 1 270 6071270607 primes below 2 ×1072×107, and for every modulus 𝑡 ≤20t≤20 and every residue class modulo 𝑡t, the free-pair event of Theorem 8 has witnesses running to the last usable index: the leanest class at 𝑡 =20t=20 carries 90 15090150 witnesses and the latest witness sits at index 1 270 5201270520 of 1 270 5401270540. The recorded floating-point witnesses pass the stronger two-window test over this finite range; they are numerical observations, not exact certificates or a proof of either cofinal producer. What the scan does not supply is uniformity in 𝑡t and in the cutoff. The receipt is free-pair.json. The public computation guide provides the programs, dependencies and exact replay commands for all three recorded runs, including the continued-fraction calculation above.

The remaining obligation

Problem #251 is open. The exact unresolved condition, equivalent to irrationality by Theorem 7 and the escape equivalence for the actual tail, is the following.

Problem 28 (universal prime-gap shift escape). For every ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0, prove that some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 satisfies

∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗∉ℤ.(8.1)(8.1)∑j≥1gN+h+j−gN+j2j∉Z.

Problem 29 (cofinal adjacent small mismatch). For every ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0, prove that some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 satisfies

| | |𝜎ℎ(𝑁)| | |<1,| | |𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)| | |<1,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1≠𝑔𝑁+1.(8.2)(8.2)|σh(N)|<1,|σh(N+1)|<1,gN+h+1≠gN+1.

Corollary 11 makes Problem 29 sufficient for Problem 28, and Theorem 8 supplies an equivalent target in which the offset is free. The three formulations are equivalent or ordered by implication; none of them is an analytic saving on its own.

What the proved obstructions leave. By Theorem 18 no hypothesis stable under bounded residue-preserving perturbation can work; by Corollary 22 adding fixed-block polynomial nonconcentration to that list does not repair it; the construction in Section 6.6 shows that recurring gap values differing by 22 in every residue class do not work at the level of integer recurrences; and by Theorem 23 the event in (8.2) has density zero, so it must be produced cofinally on a sparse set. Isolated small gaps, isolated large gaps and average gap estimates are insufficient. Any prescribed finite prefix can be preserved while the complete sum is rationalised, so that prefix alone cannot force irrationality or a cofinal small-tail producer. A finite block together with a proved tail bound can still certify one window: both inequalities in (8.2) contain the complete infinite continuation, and Proposition 14 supplies the corresponding finite reduction. Nor does parity help, since after the first gap every 𝑔𝑛gn is even.

The finite reduction is available. Proposition 14 turns each window condition into an integer comparison at truncation length 𝐿L, and for fixed ℎh and 𝜀 >0ε>0 the choice 𝐿 =⌈(4 +𝜀)log2⁡(𝑁 +2)⌉L=⌈(4+ε)log2⁡(N+2)⌉ makes 𝐸ℎ,𝑁,𝐿 =𝑂ℎ(𝑁−𝜀)Eh,N,L=Oh(N−ε). A prescribed positive margin 𝜂ℎηh therefore converts (8.2) into a statement about the joint distribution modulo powers of two of the finite block (𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1,…,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝐿 −𝑔𝑁+𝐿)(gN+h+1−gN+1,…,gN+h+L−gN+L) over a window of logarithmic length. Deciding one instance costs 𝑂(log⁡𝑁)O(log⁡N) gaps together with the elementary prime bound; producing them cofinally, with uniformity in ℎh and in the cutoff, is the open work.

The strongest published results on prime gaps address a different shape of question. Zhang’s bounded-gap theorem [15] produces infinitely many bounded consecutive-prime gaps. Maynard bounds lim inf𝑛(𝑝𝑛+𝑚 −𝑝𝑛)lim infn(pn+m−pn) for every fixed 𝑚m, giving bounded clusters of every fixed size [12], with the explicit unconditional bound lim inf𝑛(𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛) ≤600lim infn(pn+1−pn)≤600 . The large-gap theorem of Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao gives an effective lower bound for the largest single consecutive-prime gap below 𝑋X [6]. A theorem giving bounded clusters at each fixed cluster size does not by itself supply a weighted condition on windows whose length grows with the basepoint, and none of these results is used as a proof input here.

Conditionally the picture is different. Tao’s comment names uniform quantitative prime-tuples control of about log⁡log⁡𝑛log⁡log⁡n consecutive gaps as the plausible route [17], and Land’s draft carries that out under Kuperberg’s uniform prime-tuples conjecture . The obstructions of Section 6 say which unconditional substitutes cannot replace that hypothesis.

What remains to be formalised.

The two finite certificates of Propositions 14 and 15, the continued-fraction exclusion of Theorem 17, the nonconcentration transfer of Theorem 21 with its corollary, the sparsity statement of Theorem 23, and the construction of Theorem 24 are ordinary mathematical proofs with exact arithmetic replay and no Lean declaration. Everything else linked above is checked by the kernel at the pinned commit.

An elementary polynomial bound for the primes

We prove 𝑝𝑛 ≤1250(𝑛 +1)4pn≤1250(n+1)4 for every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0. Let 𝜋(𝑥)π(x) count the primes at most 𝑥x. For an integer 𝑚 ≥4m≥4,

Integer certificates

The following calculation uses trial division and integer arithmetic only. It reproduces the two rows of Proposition 15 and every inequality used in Theorem 16. The four literals are the certificate the Lean kernel decides in KernelDenominatorFloor.lean; their use here requires no floating-point approximation. Adjacent quoted strings are concatenated by Python.

from math import isqrt

primes = [n for n in range(2, 10000)
          if all(n % d for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1))]
gaps = [q - p for p, q in zip(primes, primes[1:])]
P = lambda x: x**4 + 8*x**3 + 36*x*x + 104*x + 150
Q = 2**40
expected = [(-662838684750, 11764181250),
            (873345886050, 12805761250)]
for N, target in zip((2, 3), expected):
    D = sum((gaps[N+1+j] - gaps[N+j])*2**(40-j)
            for j in range(1, 41))
    B = 1250*(P(N+43) + P(N+42))
    distance = min(D % Q, Q - D % Q)
    if (D, B) != target or not (abs(D)+B < Q and B < distance):
        raise ArithmeticError("tail certificate failed")
if gaps[4] == gaps[3]:
    raise ArithmeticError("gap mismatch failed")

u = int(
    "8065641857152652932176019632186898003271162829171466334827"
    "3083607794415278717445033509407855988903369988525550746159"
    "7355889792250084202344821020139160956663658789718168152662"
    "0217"
)

v = int(
    "2194945124413663232143970924541263312422069524635615360518"
    "4247077351958221816830720189289904831662955084392690248683"
    "1216291723988537733235173040607254496838530213867781442335"
    "1745"
)

up = int(
    "6539437101498162626882411892470905222108260008568555445975"
    "3026163315521784668689909712759876562484620059098138417469"
    "5232839888185316374272333277389611483117334000493867584923"
    "912"
)

vp = int(
    "1779611075789866551198427241621709630120136323281598176637"
    "8490605249229735501968764904036152970729491656650873938580"
    "6203025466313389810291243786005499164537499383612081805160"
    "767"
)

c = len(primes)
A = sum(p*2**(c-1-i) for i, p in enumerate(primes))
checks = (c == 1229,
          u > 0 and v > 0 and up > 0 and vp > 0,
          up*v - u*vp == 1,
          u*2**c < A*v,
          (2*A + 5000*(c+1)**4)*vp < up*2**(c+1),
          v+vp >= 2**589,
          2**589 > 10**177)
if not all(checks):
    raise ArithmeticError("denominator certificate failed")
print("Both tail rows and the denominator floor verified.")

Guide to the formal sources

Each linked phrase opens its Lean declaration at the pinned source revision ee650b32b8b2. The summation-by-parts and prime-bound declarations are prime-specific. Section 3 is stated for arbitrary integer digits and arbitrary rational or real orbits, while Section 4 records the actual-gap specialisation. The concrete prime-gap tail, its unconditional convergence, its recurrence and the real-to-rational scaled-tail bridge are defined and checked in RealPrimeGapTail.lean and PrimeGapDyadicTail.lean; the free-pair lattice and its actual-series equivalence in FreePairReduction.lean; the kernel-decided denominator certificate in KernelDenominatorFloor.lean; the rational countermodels in BoundedPerturbationCountermodel.lean and PolynomialGapSeriesValue.lean; and the two circularity theorems in AffineCylinderCollapse.lean, with the signed normal form in AffineShiftEscape.lean and the lcm diagonal in OrderLatticeDiagonal.lean.

The totient witness and forward propagation

The note states the exact denominator law (3.1) and uses it directly. The classical witness that produced it is worth recording, because it is the form in which the shift length first appears.

Proposition 30 (a shift of totient length). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits. If the reduced denominator 𝑑d of 𝑇𝑁TN is odd, then 𝜎𝜑(𝑑)(𝑁)σφ(d)(N) is an integer.

Proof. Since 𝑑d is odd, 22 and 𝑑d are coprime, so Euler’s congruence gives 𝑑 ∣2𝜑(𝑑) −1d∣2φ(d)−1. Writing 2𝜑(𝑑) −1 =𝑑𝑘2φ(d)−1=dk and 𝑇𝑁 =𝑢/𝑑TN=u/d in lowest terms, (2𝜑(𝑑) −1)𝑇𝑁 =𝑘𝑢(2φ(d)−1)TN=ku is an integer, and the integral-shift criterion transfers this to the shift. ◻

Proposition 31 (propagation). If 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is an integer, then 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +𝑘)σh(N+k) is an integer for every 𝑘 ≥0k≥0.

Proof. The shift step identity gives 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1) =2𝜎ℎ(𝑁) −(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1)σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1), an integer combination of an integer and two digits. Induct on 𝑘k. ◻

These are the totient shift and the propagation theorems cited in the note. Two worked instances. If den⁡𝑇𝑁 =3den⁡TN=3 then 𝜑(3) =2φ(3)=2 and 3𝑇𝑁3TN is an integer, so 𝜎2(𝑁)σ2(N) is integral while 𝜎1(𝑁)σ1(N) is not; if den⁡𝑇𝑁 =5den⁡TN=5 then 𝜎4(𝑁)σ4(N) is integral. In the orbit with every digit zero and 𝑇0 =1/12T0=1/12, the denominator is 12 =22 ⋅312=22⋅3, the orbit reaches 𝑇2 =1/3T2=1/3 with odd denominator at 𝑠 =2s=2, and ℎ =𝜑(3) =2h=φ(3)=2 is exactly the shift length seen to be integral from index 22 onwards. The totient is a witness rather than the classification: the exact criterion is den⁡(𝑇𝑁) ∣2ℎ −1den⁡(TN)∣2h−1, and the least admissible ℎh is the multiplicative order of 22 modulo the odd part.

Divisor-hitting shift escape

Problem 33 (divisor-hitting shift escape). For every 𝑟 ≥1r≥1, does some positive multiple of 𝑟r escape cofinally, in the sense of (8.1) at shift length 𝑚𝑟mr for some 𝑚 ≥1m≥1?

This is an exact reformulation, not a weaker mathematical target. If 𝑇0T0 is irrational, every positive shift is nonintegral by the block identity, so divisor-hitting escape follows with 𝑚 =1m=1. Conversely, rationality gives a shift ℎ ≥1h≥1 that is integral at every sufficiently late index. For each positive integer 𝑚m, the identity

𝑇𝑁+𝑚ℎ−𝑇𝑁=𝑚−1∑𝑗=0(𝑇𝑁+(𝑗+1)ℎ−𝑇𝑁+𝑗ℎ)TN+mh−TN=∑j=0m−1(TN+(j+1)h−TN+jh)

makes every multiple 𝑚ℎmh eventually integral. Taking 𝑟 =ℎr=h contradicts divisor-hitting escape. This ordinary deduction uses the checked rationality classification and a finite telescope; rearranging the quantifiers supplies no new estimate for the actual prime gaps.

Two ordinary proofs about the free-pair producer

Both arguments below are ordinary mathematical deductions. The first uses the prime number theorem, while the second consumes the free-pair lattice proved above. Neither deduction is claimed to be kernel-checked; the exact tail recurrence and free-pair statements they use have their separate linked Lean evidence.

Exchanging the order of summation gives ∑𝑁≤𝑋𝑇𝑁 ≤(𝑝𝑋+1 −𝑝0) +2𝑇𝑋∑N≤XTN≤(pX+1−p0)+2TX. The prime number theorem [13] also gives

for all large 𝑋X. Thus, for each fixed 𝐶 >1C>1, Markov’s inequality leaves at least (1 −1/𝐶)𝑋(1−1/C)X indices in (𝑋,2𝑋](X,2X] with 𝑇𝑁 ≤𝐾0𝐶log⁡𝑋TN≤K0Clog⁡X.

Under rationality, take 𝑋X beyond the point where the reduced denominator is the fixed odd integer 𝑑d. On this set 𝑇𝑁TN lies in 𝑑−1ℤ≥0d−1Z≥0 and takes at most 𝑑𝐾0𝐶log⁡𝑋 +1dK0Clog⁡X+1 values. Pigeonhole therefore gives one value at ≫𝐶,𝑑𝑋/log⁡𝑋≫C,dX/log⁡X indices. This compression uses the growth of the actual primes. It is false for a general rational integer-digit orbit: the quadratic countermodel of Proposition 25 has the strictly increasing tails 𝑇𝑁 =2(𝑁 +4)2TN=2(N+4)2. Even for the primes, equal-tail pairs have difference zero and hence do not supply the nonintegral difference required by the free-pair criterion. The naive form ∑𝑁≤𝑋𝑇𝑁 ≤𝑝𝑋+1∑N≤XTN≤pX+1 is false.

Redundancy of the gap condition.

Under the free-pair lattice the difference 𝑇𝑀 −𝑇𝑁TM−TN is an integer whenever the modulus divides the offset, and an integer cannot lie in (12,1)(12,1). The half-window component of the reduced event of Theorem 13 is therefore already a contradiction on its own, and the gap-mismatch condition adds nothing to it. That changes which component a proof has to produce.

Corrections to earlier records

The superseded exclusion.

An earlier internal record narrated a denominator exclusion at 1060210602. That figure is correct as written and is superseded twice over: by the kernel-decided floor 2589 >101772589>10177 of Theorem 16, which is smaller but kernel-checked, and by the certified continued-fraction exclusion 239997 >1012040239997>1012040 of Theorem 17, which supersedes it in strength. The receipt records the decimal digit count 1204112041; the certified decimal statement uses the exponent 1204012040.

The named missing input.

An earlier record named Hardy-Littlewood 𝑘k-tuple correlation of consecutive gaps at a fixed offset as the missing input. With the offset freed by Theorem 8 the route needs, for each modulus 𝑡t, cofinally many congruent pairs with certified nonintegral tail difference. A further record proposed that two even values differing by 22, each occurring infinitely often inside a common index residue class, would supply the two-condition form. No proof of that implication was ever produced, and Theorem 24 shows that no proof exists at the level of integer-digit recurrences. That entry is withdrawn.

The formal boundary.

An earlier reading of the short note placed the real-tail bridge and the real form of the adjacent-pair consumer on the paper side. Both are kernel-checked, at line 48 and line 99 of the real prime-gap tail module. A second reading placed the kernel-decided denominator floor and the free-pair criterion outside the source revision the note pins. Both modules are present at that revision, and both are linked from the note.

Dyadic tail integrality classification

Reader position. 11 of 70; display band: major result. Formal editorial disposition: merge. These are separate classifications.

Reader entry. For any integer-digit dyadic tail recurrence T(N+1) = 2*T(N) - g(N+1), the rational h-shift is integral exactly when the reduced denominator of T(N) divides 2^h - 1, equivalently when 2^h is congruent to 1 modulo that denominator. For the real recurrence, the load-bearing normal form says that irrationality of T(0) is equivalent to every positive tail shift being nonintegral; the eventual-integrality equivalence and denominator/order laws are supporting mechanism evidence.

For the real recurrence, the load-bearing normal form says that irrationality of T(0) is equivalent to every positive tail shift being nonintegral; the eventual-integrality equivalence and denominator/order laws are supporting mechanism evidence.

The representative assumes T : ℕN →→ ℚQ, the DyadicTailRecurrence for the actual prime-gap digits, and for every N00 an N ≥≥ N00 whose adjacent h-shifts both lie strictly in (-1, 1) while the corresponding prime gaps differ. This is a conditional reduction only: no #251 irrationality, infinite rational-sum limit, universal producer, novelty, priority, significance, or external-review claim is made; #251 remains open.
